```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL, seasonal_decompose
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf

DATA_PATH = Path.home() / "Documents/GitHub/Data_Analytics/data"
assert DATA_PATH.exists(), f"Data directory not found: {DATA_PATH}"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="talk")
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (10, 5)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20)
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)

COLORS = {
    "data": "#6B7280",
    "trend": "#D55E00",
    "seasonal": "#0072B2",
    "remainder": "#009E73",
    "adjusted": "#CC79A7",
}

COLORS = {
    "data": "#6B7280",
    "adjusted": "#CC79A7",
    "observed": "#6B7280",
    "trend": "#D55E00",
    "seasonal": "#0072B2",
    "remainder": "#009E73",
    "outlier": "#CC3311",
    "missing": "#CC79A7",
    "imputed": "#E69F00",
}


def time_plot(df, x, y, *, title, xlabel, ylabel, color="#0072B2",
              label=None, ax=None, figsize=(10, 5), linewidth=1.2):
    """Version-stable Matplotlib helper; avoids plot_series API changes."""
    if ax is None:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    else:
        fig = ax.figure
    ax.plot(df[x], df[y], color=color, label=label, linewidth=linewidth)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel=xlabel, ylabel=ylabel)
    if label is not None:
        ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, ax

def component_plot(frame, *, title, observed="data", trend="trend",
                   seasonal="seasonal", remainder="remainder"):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(11, 7))
    specifications = [
        (observed, "Observed", COLORS["data"]),
        (trend, "Trend-cycle", COLORS["trend"]),
        (seasonal, "Seasonal", COLORS["seasonal"]),
        (remainder, "Remainder", COLORS["remainder"]),
    ]
    for ax, (column, label, color) in zip(axes, specifications):
        ax.plot(frame["ds"], frame[column], color=color, linewidth=1)
        ax.set_ylabel(label)
    axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time")
    fig.suptitle(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, axes
  
def plot_series_matplotlib(df, *, x="ds", y="y", title="", xlabel="Time",
                           ylabel="Value", color="#0072B2", ax=None):
    """Stable plotting helper that does not depend on utilsforecast APIs."""
    if ax is None:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    else:
        fig = ax.figure
    ax.plot(df[x], df[y], color=color, linewidth=1.3)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel=xlabel, ylabel=ylabel)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, ax
```

# Introduction

## Why decompose a time series?

A time series can combine several visual structures:

- long-run movement;
- seasonal repetition;
- cycles;
- irregular fluctuations;
- calendar and scale effects.

Decomposition separates these layers so they can be inspected individually.

::: {.notes}
Decomposition is a visual and analytical device. It supports understanding and may also improve forecasting by isolating structures that require different treatment.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Three conceptual components

We usually combine trend and cycle into a **trend-cycle** component:

$$
y_t = \text{trend-cycle} + \text{seasonal} + \text{remainder}.
$$

For high-frequency series, more than one seasonal component may be present.

::: {.notes}
The remainder is not automatically white noise. It is what remains after the selected decomposition procedure and parameter settings.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of the lecture, students will be able to:

- distinguish transformations from decomposition;
- explain additive and multiplicative structures;
- calculate and visualize moving averages;
- construct classical additive and multiplicative decompositions;
- explain seasonal adjustment;
- identify limitations of classical decomposition;
- apply and tune STL;
- diagnose leakage, outliers, and unstable seasonality;
- communicate components without misleading scales.

::: {.notes}
The emphasis is visual reasoning supported by mathematically precise definitions and executable Python.
:::

## Analytical sequence

```text
RAW SERIES
    ↓
KNOWN ADJUSTMENTS
    ↓
TRANSFORMATION / SCALE CHOICE
    ↓
TREND-CYCLE EXTRACTION
    ↓
SEASONAL EXTRACTION
    ↓
REMAINDER DIAGNOSTICS
    ↓
SEASONALLY ADJUSTED SERIES
```

::: {.notes}
Each arrow represents a modeling choice. Different choices can produce different component estimates.
:::

# Transformations and Adjustments

## Why adjust before decomposing?

Adjustments can remove known or interpretable sources of variation:

- calendar composition;
- population growth;
- inflation;
- changing variance with the level.

The goal is a simpler, more stable structure.

::: {.notes}
An adjustment is justified by measurement and domain knowledge. It is not merely a cosmetic operation.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Calendar adjustment

If monthly totals depend partly on the number of trading days, use a rate:

$$
\text{sales per trading day}_t = \frac{\text{monthly sales}_t}{\text{trading days}_t}.
$$

```{python}
calendar_demo = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": pd.period_range("2026-01", periods=6, freq="M").astype(str),
    "total_sales": [220, 190, 235, 228, 242, 215],
    "trading_days": [22, 19, 22, 21, 22, 20],
})
calendar_demo["sales_per_day"] = (
    calendar_demo["total_sales"] / calendar_demo["trading_days"]
)
calendar_demo
```

::: {.notes}
The chapter uses trading days as an example of calendar variation that can be removed before further analysis.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Totals and rates tell different stories

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].bar(calendar_demo["month"], calendar_demo["total_sales"], color="#56B4E9")
axes[0].set(title="Monthly total", ylabel="Sales")
axes[1].bar(calendar_demo["month"], calendar_demo["sales_per_day"], color="#009E73")
axes[1].set(title="Per trading day", ylabel="Sales per day")
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The adjustment changes the estimand. The chart title and axis units must make that explicit.
:::

## Population adjustment

For totals affected by population size:

$$
\text{per-capita quantity}_t
=
\frac{\text{total quantity}_t}{\text{population}_t}.
$$


```{python}
global_economy = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "global_economy.csv")
australia = (
    global_economy.loc[lambda x: x["unique_id"] == "Australia"]
    .assign(GDP_per_capita=lambda x: x["GDP"] / x["Population"])
)
australia[["ds", "GDP", "Population", "GDP_per_capita"]].head()
```

::: {.notes}
A total can increase while a per-capita quantity decreases if population grows more rapidly.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

##  Australian GDP per capita

```{python}
fig, ax = time_plot(
    australia, "ds", "GDP_per_capita",
    title="GDP per capita: Australia",
    xlabel="Year [1Y]", ylabel="US dollars",
)
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The visual question is no longer the size of the whole economy, but economic output relative to population.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Inflation adjustment

Let $y_t$ be a nominal value and $z_t$ a price index. In base-period prices:

$$
x_t = \frac{y_t}{z_t}z_{\text{base}}.
$$

If the index equals 100 in the base period:

$$
x_t = y_t\frac{100}{z_t}.
$$

::: {.notes}
The adjusted series measures values in constant purchasing-power units. The price index, base period, and currency must be reported.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Nominal versus real visualization

```{python}
inflation_demo = pd.DataFrame({
    "year": np.arange(2010, 2026),
    "nominal": 100 * 1.055 ** np.arange(16),
    "cpi": 100 * 1.035 ** np.arange(16),
})
inflation_demo["real_2010"] = inflation_demo["nominal"] * 100 / inflation_demo["cpi"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(inflation_demo["year"], inflation_demo["nominal"], label="Nominal", linewidth=2)
ax.plot(inflation_demo["year"], inflation_demo["real_2010"], label="Real, 2010 prices", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="Nominal and inflation-adjusted series", xlabel="Year", ylabel="Index")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
This is a synthetic illustration. Inflation adjustment can reveal weaker real growth than nominal growth.
:::

## Mathematical transformation

When variation grows with the level, a log transformation may stabilize relative variation:

$$
w_t = \log(y_t), \qquad y_t>0.
$$

A change on the log scale corresponds to a relative change on the original scale:

$$
\log(y_t)-\log(y_{t-1})
=
\log\left(\frac{y_t}{y_{t-1}}\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
Natural logarithms are used throughout the Box-Cox discussion. Logs require strictly positive observations.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Original scale versus log scale

```{python}
aus_production = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
gas = aus_production[["ds", "Gas"]].dropna().copy()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(gas["ds"], gas["Gas"], color="#0072B2")
axes[0].set(title="Australian gas production", xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Gas")
axes[1].plot(gas["ds"], np.log(gas["Gas"]), color="#009E73")
axes[1].set(title="Log-transformed gas production", xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="log(Gas)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare whether seasonal amplitude appears more stable after transformation. Do not interpret log units as original gas units.
:::

## Modified Box-Cox family

The chapter uses a modified Box-Cox transformation:

$$
w_t=
\begin{cases}
\log(y_t), & \lambda=0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\operatorname{sign}(y_t)|y_t|^\lambda-1}{\lambda},
& \lambda\ne0.
\end{cases}
$$

For the standard positive-data Box-Cox transformation, $y_t>0$ is required.

::: {.notes}
At lambda equal to one, the transformed series is shifted by one without changing shape. Other lambda values change the shape and scale.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Visual effect of lambda

```{python}
lambdas = [1.0, 0.5, 0.0, -0.5]
positive_gas = gas.loc[gas["Gas"] > 0].copy()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7), sharex=True)
for ax, lam in zip(axes.flat, lambdas):
    transformed = np.log(positive_gas["Gas"]) if lam == 0 else stats.boxcox(positive_gas["Gas"], lmbda=lam)
    ax.plot(positive_gas["ds"], transformed, color="#0072B2", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_title(f"λ = {lam:g}")
fig.suptitle("Box-Cox transformations of Australian gas production")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
This code uses SciPy's standard positive-data Box-Cox implementation. The selection goal is a transformation that makes seasonal variation and variance more stable.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Data-driven lambda: document the criterion

```{python}
lambda_mle = stats.boxcox_normmax(positive_gas["Gas"], method="mle")
lambda_mle
```

This is a maximum-likelihood choice from SciPy, **not** the Guerrero criterion used in the chapter's `boxcox_lambda()` example.

::: {.notes}
Different selection criteria estimate lambda for different goals. The criterion must be named rather than presented as a universal optimum.
:::

# Time Series Components

## Additive decomposition

$$
y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t.
$$

Appropriate when seasonal amplitude and remainder variation are roughly stable across the level of the series.

::: {.notes}
T is trend-cycle, S seasonality, and R remainder. The equality is a structural representation; estimated components are denoted with hats.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Multiplicative decomposition

$$
y_t = T_t\times S_t\times R_t.
$$

Appropriate when seasonal or remainder variation is approximately proportional to the series level.

Taking logs converts multiplication into addition:

$$
\log y_t = \log T_t + \log S_t + \log R_t.
$$

::: {.notes}
Multiplicative components are ratios or indices, not additive quantities in the original unit.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Additive or multiplicative? Look at amplitude

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
idx = pd.date_range("2010-01-01", periods=120, freq="MS")
t = np.arange(120)
additive = 100 + .3*t + 10*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/12)
multiplicative = (100 + .3*t) * (1 + .12*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/12))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].plot(idx, additive); axes[0].set_title("Constant seasonal amplitude")
axes[1].plot(idx, multiplicative); axes[1].set_title("Seasonal amplitude grows with level")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
These are synthetic pedagogical examples. The left suggests additive structure; the right suggests multiplicative structure or a stabilizing transformation.
:::

## US retail employment

```{python}
us_employment = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "us_employment.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
us_retail_employment = us_employment.loc[
    lambda x: (x["unique_id"] == "Retail Trade") & (x["ds"] >= "1990")
].copy()
us_retail_employment.head()
```

::: {.notes}
This monthly series is the chapter's main decomposition example.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Total employment in US retail

```{python}
fig, ax = time_plot(
    us_retail_employment, "ds", "y",
    title="Total employment in US retail",
    xlabel="Month [1M]", ylabel="Persons (thousands)",
)
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Before decomposing, ask students to identify long-run movement, repeating seasonal peaks, changing behavior, and unusual periods.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## STL decomposition object

```{python}
stl_default = STL(us_retail_employment["y"], period=12)
res_default = stl_default.fit()
dcmp = pd.DataFrame({
    "ds": us_retail_employment["ds"].to_numpy(),
    "data": us_retail_employment["y"].to_numpy(),
    "trend": res_default.trend,
    "seasonal": res_default.seasonal,
    "remainder": res_default.resid,
})
dcmp.head()
```

::: {.notes}
The decomposition estimates components. It does not reveal uniquely observable truths; estimates depend on method and smoothing choices.
:::

## Data and trend-cycle

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["data"], color=COLORS["data"], label="Data", linewidth=1)
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["trend"], color=COLORS["trend"], label="Trend-cycle", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="Total employment in US retail", xlabel="Month [1M]", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The trend-cycle follows broad movement while filtering seasonal and short-run fluctuations.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## STL components

```{python}
fig, axes = component_plot(dcmp, title="STL decomposition of US retail employment")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Panel scales differ. A component that fills its panel is not necessarily large relative to the observed series. Always inspect axis values.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Seasonally adjusted series

For an additive decomposition:

$$
y_t^{\mathrm{SA}} = y_t-\widehat S_t
=\widehat T_t+\widehat R_t.
$$

For a multiplicative decomposition:

$$
y_t^{\mathrm{SA}}=\frac{y_t}{\widehat S_t}.
$$

::: {.notes}
Seasonally adjusted does not mean smooth because the remainder remains. For turning points, the trend-cycle is usually the clearer visual object.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Seasonally adjusted versus trend-cycle

```{python}
dcmp["seasonally_adjusted"] = dcmp["data"] - dcmp["seasonal"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["seasonally_adjusted"], color=COLORS["adjusted"],
        label="Seasonally adjusted", linewidth=1)
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["trend"], color=COLORS["trend"],
        label="Trend-cycle", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="Seasonally adjusted series is not the trend", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Short-run movements in the seasonally adjusted series can come from the remainder. Do not interpret every movement as a change in trend.
:::

# 3.3 Moving Averages

## Centered moving average of odd order

For $m=2k+1$:

$$
\widehat T_t
=
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{j=-k}^{k}y_{t+j}.
$$

Nearby observations are averaged to suppress short-run fluctuations.

::: {.notes}
Odd order produces a symmetric centered window. Estimates are unavailable near endpoints without additional rules.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Australian exports

```{python}
aus_exports = (
    global_economy.loc[lambda x: x["unique_id"] == "Australia"]
    .assign(MA_5=lambda x: x["Exports"].rolling(5, center=True).mean())
)
aus_exports[["ds", "Exports", "MA_5"]].head(8)
```

::: {.notes}
The first 5-MA estimate averages five years centered on the corresponding year.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Exports and 5-MA

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(aus_exports["ds"], aus_exports["Exports"], color="black", label="Exports")
ax.plot(aus_exports["ds"], aus_exports["MA_5"], color=COLORS["trend"], label="5-MA", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="Total Australian exports", xlabel="Year [1Y]", ylabel="% of GDP")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The moving average reveals broad movement but omits two observations at each end for a centered 5-term window.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Smoothness depends on order

```{python}
for window in [3, 5, 9, 15]:
    aus_exports[f"MA_{window}"] = aus_exports["Exports"].rolling(window, center=True).mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(aus_exports["ds"], aus_exports["Exports"], color="0.75", label="Data")
for window, color in zip([3, 5, 9, 15], sns.color_palette("viridis", 4)):
    ax.plot(aus_exports["ds"], aus_exports[f"MA_{window}"], label=f"{window}-MA", color=color)
ax.set(title="Moving-average order controls smoothness", xlabel="Year", ylabel="Exports (% GDP)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Larger windows smooth more strongly but can obscure turning points and create longer endpoint gaps.
:::

## Moving average of moving averages

Quarterly seasonality has even period $m=4$. A centered $2\times4$ moving average is obtained by applying a 2-MA after a 4-MA.

```{python}
beer = (
    aus_production[["ds", "Beer"]]
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"] >= "1992"]
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
beer["4-MA"] = beer["Beer"].rolling(4, center=True).mean().shift(-1)
beer["2x4-MA"] = beer["4-MA"].rolling(2, center=True).mean()
beer.head(8)
```

::: {.notes}
The second moving average restores symmetry for an even seasonal window.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Equivalent weighted average

The $2\times4$-MA is

$$
\widehat T_t
=
\frac18y_{t-2}
+
\frac14y_{t-1}
+
\frac14y_t
+
\frac14y_{t+1}
+
\frac18y_{t+2}.
$$

The weights are symmetric and sum to one.

::: {.notes}
Combining simple moving averages creates a weighted moving average with smaller weights at the endpoints.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Trend extraction should match seasonal period

- quarterly, $m=4$: use a centered $2\times4$-MA;
- monthly, $m=12$: use a centered $2\times12$-MA;
- daily with weekly seasonality, $m=7$: use a 7-MA.

A mismatched window can leave seasonal oscillation in the trend estimate.

::: {.notes}
The window is not selected only for visual smoothness. It is aligned with the seasonal period to average out the seasonal positions.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## 2x12-MA for retail employment

```{python}
ma_employment = us_retail_employment.copy()
ma_employment["12-MA"] = ma_employment["y"].rolling(12, center=True).mean().shift(-1)
ma_employment["2x12-MA"] = ma_employment["12-MA"].rolling(2, center=True).mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ma_employment["ds"], ma_employment["y"], color="0.7", label="Data")
ax.plot(ma_employment["ds"], ma_employment["2x12-MA"], color=COLORS["trend"], label="2x12-MA", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="Total employment in US retail", xlabel="Month [1M]", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The centered moving average largely removes annual seasonality but has no estimates at the ends.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

# 3.4 Classical Decomposition

## Classical additive algorithm

For seasonal period $m$:

1. estimate $\widehat T_t$ with an $m$-MA or centered $2\times m$-MA;
2. detrend: $d_t=y_t-\widehat T_t$;
3. average $d_t$ by seasonal position and normalize so seasonal factors sum to zero;
4. calculate

$$
\widehat R_t=y_t-\widehat T_t-\widehat S_t.
$$

::: {.notes}
The seasonal pattern is assumed constant from cycle to cycle.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Classical additive decomposition in Python

```{python}
classical_add = seasonal_decompose(
    us_retail_employment.set_index("ds")["y"],
    model="additive", period=12, extrapolate_trend=0,
)
classical_frame = pd.DataFrame({
    "ds": us_retail_employment["ds"].to_numpy(),
    "data": us_retail_employment["y"].to_numpy(),
    "trend": classical_add.trend.to_numpy(),
    "seasonal": classical_add.seasonal.to_numpy(),
    "remainder": classical_add.resid.to_numpy(),
})
```

::: {.notes}
The statsmodels function operationalizes classical decomposition. Missing trend and remainder values at the endpoints are retained to make the limitation visible.
:::

## Classical additive components

```{python}
fig, axes = component_plot(classical_frame, title="Classical additive decomposition")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare this with STL. Classical seasonality repeats exactly and endpoint estimates are absent.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Classical multiplicative algorithm

1. estimate $\widehat T_t$;
2. detrend: $d_t=y_t/\widehat T_t$;
3. average ratios by season and normalize so seasonal indices sum to $m$;
4. calculate

$$
\widehat R_t
=
\frac{y_t}{\widehat T_t\widehat S_t}.
$$

::: {.notes}
Multiplicative seasonal indices average to one, equivalently sum to m across one full seasonal cycle.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Multiplicative decomposition of gas

```{python}
recent_gas = gas.tail(5 * 4).set_index("ds")["Gas"]
classical_mult = seasonal_decompose(recent_gas, model="multiplicative", period=4)
mult_frame = pd.DataFrame({
    "ds": recent_gas.index,
    "data": recent_gas.to_numpy(),
    "trend": classical_mult.trend.to_numpy(),
    "seasonal": classical_mult.seasonal.to_numpy(),
    "remainder": classical_mult.resid.to_numpy(),
})
fig, axes = component_plot(mult_frame, title="Classical multiplicative decomposition of gas")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Interpret the seasonal and remainder panels as ratios around one, not quantities in the original gas unit.
:::

## Limitations of classical decomposition

- no trend-cycle or remainder estimates near endpoints;
- rapid rises and falls can be over-smoothed;
- seasonality is forced to repeat exactly;
- changing seasonal patterns cannot be represented;
- unusual observations can distort components.

::: {.notes}
The chapter explicitly does not recommend classical decomposition when better methods are available, although it remains useful for understanding the logic.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Outlier contamination experiment

```{python}
gas_outlier = recent_gas.copy()
gas_outlier.iloc[len(gas_outlier)//2] += 300
base_dec = seasonal_decompose(recent_gas, model="multiplicative", period=4)
out_dec = seasonal_decompose(gas_outlier, model="multiplicative", period=4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(recent_gas.index, recent_gas / base_dec.seasonal, label="Original adjusted")
ax.plot(gas_outlier.index, gas_outlier / out_dec.seasonal, label="With outlier adjusted", alpha=.8)
ax.set(title="Classical seasonal adjustment is sensitive to unusual values", xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Seasonally adjusted gas")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The extreme value can influence the estimated trend and seasonal indices, spreading its impact beyond a single period.
:::

# 3.5 Official Seasonal Adjustment

## X-11 and SEATS

Official statistical agencies commonly use variants of:

- **X-11**, based on classical decomposition with additional procedures;
- **SEATS**, Seasonal Extraction in ARIMA Time Series;
- combinations of both.

They are designed primarily for monthly and quarterly official series.

::: {.notes}
The chapter states that these procedures are not intended for daily, hourly, or weekly seasonality.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## What X-11 adds

The chapter highlights that X-11:

- provides endpoint trend-cycle estimates;
- allows slowly changing seasonality;
- handles trading-day and holiday variation;
- can include known predictors;
- supports additive and multiplicative forms;
- is designed to be robust to outliers and level shifts.

::: {.notes}
This slide summarizes capabilities explicitly described in the chapter. The detailed X-11 algorithm is beyond this lecture.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

# STL Decomposition

## What is STL?

**STL** means **Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess**.

STL estimates:

- a smooth trend-cycle;
- a seasonal component that may evolve;
- a remainder;
- optionally robust weights for unusual observations.

::: {.notes}
LOESS is a local regression smoother. STL was introduced by Cleveland and coauthors and later extended to multiple seasonal patterns through MSTL.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Advantages and limitations

### Advantages

- supports many seasonal periods, not only monthly or quarterly;
- seasonal evolution is controllable;
- trend smoothness is controllable;
- robust fitting can protect trend and seasonality from outliers.

### Limitations

- does not automatically handle trading-day or calendar effects;
- directly provides additive decomposition only.

::: {.notes}
A multiplicative interpretation can be approached by logging positive data before STL.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Robust STL

```{python}
stl_robust = STL(
    us_retail_employment["y"],
    period=12,
    seasonal=13,
    trend=21,
    robust=True,
)
res_robust = stl_robust.fit()
robust_frame = pd.DataFrame({
    "ds": us_retail_employment["ds"].to_numpy(),
    "data": us_retail_employment["y"].to_numpy(),
    "trend": res_robust.trend,
    "seasonal": res_robust.seasonal,
    "remainder": res_robust.resid,
})
```

::: {.notes}
The seasonal and trend windows are odd integers. Smaller values permit more rapid component changes.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Robust STL components

```{python}
fig, axes = component_plot(robust_frame, title="Robust STL decomposition with flexible trend")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare the remainder around the global financial crisis with the default decomposition. A too-rigid trend can leak systematic movement into the remainder.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Trend-window sensitivity

```{python}
trend_windows = [21, 37, 61]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(us_retail_employment["ds"], us_retail_employment["y"], color="0.85", label="Data")
for window, color in zip(trend_windows, sns.color_palette("viridis", 3)):
    fit = STL(us_retail_employment["y"], period=12, seasonal=13,
              trend=window, robust=True).fit()
    ax.plot(us_retail_employment["ds"], fit.trend, label=f"trend={window}", color=color)
ax.set(title="STL trend window controls flexibility", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Smaller trend windows allow more rapid changes. Larger windows produce smoother trends but may push signal into the remainder.
:::

## Seasonal-window sensitivity

```{python}
seasonal_windows = [7, 13, 25]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(11, 7))
for ax, window, color in zip(axes, seasonal_windows, sns.color_palette("viridis", 3)):
    fit = STL(us_retail_employment["y"], period=12, seasonal=window,
              trend=21, robust=True).fit()
    ax.plot(us_retail_employment["ds"], fit.seasonal, color=color)
    ax.set_ylabel(f"seasonal={window}")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Month")
fig.suptitle("STL seasonal window controls temporal evolution")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A smaller seasonal smoother permits the shape to evolve more rapidly; a larger one stabilizes the seasonal component.
:::

## Robust versus non-robust STL

```{python}
series_outlier = us_retail_employment["y"].copy()
position = len(series_outlier) // 2
series_outlier.iloc[position] += 2500
plain = STL(series_outlier, period=12, seasonal=13, trend=21, robust=False).fit()
robust = STL(series_outlier, period=12, seasonal=13, trend=21, robust=True).fit()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(us_retail_employment["ds"], plain.trend, label="Non-robust trend")
ax.plot(us_retail_employment["ds"], robust.trend, label="Robust trend", linewidth=2)
ax.axvline(us_retail_employment["ds"].iloc[position], color="0.4", linestyle="--", label="Injected outlier")
ax.set(title="Robust STL limits outlier influence on trend", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Robust STL does not make the outlier disappear. It seeks to keep unusual observations from distorting the trend and seasonal components, leaving the impact in the remainder.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Remainder diagnostics

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(robust_frame["ds"], robust_frame["remainder"], color=COLORS["remainder"])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="0.4", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set(title="Remainder through time", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Remainder")
plot_acf(robust_frame["remainder"].dropna(), lags=36, zero=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title="Remainder ACF", xlabel="Lag [1M]")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Look for leftover autocorrelation, changing variance, unusual observations, and unresolved seasonal peaks. The remainder need not be white noise, but visible structure indicates incomplete decomposition for the intended purpose.
:::

## Component scales can mislead

A decomposition plot usually gives each panel its own vertical scale.

Therefore:

- panel height is not component importance;
- compare axis values, not visual amplitude alone;
- annotate units and zero lines;
- use overlays when direct magnitude comparison matters.

::: {.notes}
This visual-literacy point is central to decomposition plots and appears again in the chapter exercises.
:::

## Overlay components on a common scale

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(robust_frame["ds"], robust_frame["data"], color=COLORS["data"], label="Data")
ax.plot(robust_frame["ds"], robust_frame["trend"], color=COLORS["trend"], label="Trend")
ax.plot(robust_frame["ds"], robust_frame["seasonally_adjusted"] if "seasonally_adjusted" in robust_frame else robust_frame["data"]-robust_frame["seasonal"],
        color=COLORS["adjusted"], label="Seasonally adjusted", alpha=.8)
ax.set(title="Common-scale comparison", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Persons (thousands)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A common-scale overlay clarifies the relative magnitude of trend and seasonal adjustment, but too many overlapping lines can reduce readability.
:::

# Integrated Visual Workflow

## Decomposition decision guide

| Evidence | Useful response |
|---|---|
| trading-day variation | calendar adjustment |
| total driven by population | per-capita adjustment |
| nominal monetary growth | inflation adjustment |
| amplitude grows with level | log or Box-Cox, then additive method |
| stable fixed seasonality | classical decomposition may describe it |
| evolving seasonality | STL |
| unusual observations | robust STL and explicit investigation |
| multiple seasonal periods | MSTL or another multi-seasonal method |

::: {.notes}
This guide summarizes analytical choices. It is not a substitute for inspection and domain knowledge.
:::

## Visual diagnostic protocol

1. plot the original series;
2. label units and frequency;
3. inspect seasonal amplitude against level;
4. remove known calendar, population, or price effects;
5. compare plausible transformations;
6. estimate components;
7. compare observed, trend, and adjusted series;
8. inspect remainder over time and by ACF;
9. test sensitivity to windows and robust fitting;
10. document choices and limitations.

::: {.notes}
The protocol is the reusable output of the lecture.
:::

## What decomposition does not prove

Decomposition alone does not prove:

- causality;
- that a remainder is random;
- that a trend will continue;
- that a seasonal pattern is structurally stable;
- that the selected transformation is optimal;
- that forecasts will be accurate.

::: {.notes}
Components are estimated descriptive structures, not autonomous causal mechanisms.
:::

# Practice

## Capstone exercise

Choose one local series and produce a decomposition report that:

1. defines frequency, seasonal period, and units;
2. identifies needed calendar, population, or inflation adjustments;
3. compares original and transformed scales;
4. justifies additive or multiplicative structure;
5. visualizes a moving-average trend;
6. performs classical decomposition;
7. performs robust STL;
8. compares seasonally adjusted and trend-cycle series;
9. diagnoses the remainder;
10. reports parameter sensitivity and limitations.

::: {.notes}
Suggested series include Gas from aus_production, Retail Trade from us_employment, and a positive retail series.
:::

## Guided gas exercise

Using the last five years of quarterly gas production:

- plot and describe seasonality and trend;
- calculate a multiplicative classical decomposition;
- plot seasonal indices;
- compute seasonally adjusted gas;
- insert an outlier in the middle and repeat;
- insert an outlier near an endpoint and compare;
- explain why the effect differs.

::: {.notes}
This closely follows the chapter's exercise structure while emphasizing visual comparison and outlier sensitivity.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/03-decomposition.html
:::

## Assessment rubric

| Dimension | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Mathematical precision | additive, multiplicative, MA, and adjustment formulas are correct |
| Visual reasoning | component scales and overlays are interpreted carefully |
| Transformation | scale choice is justified and units are updated |
| Seasonality | period and stability are explained |
| Robustness | outliers and parameter sensitivity are examined |
| Diagnostics | remainder is inspected through time and autocorrelation |
| Reproducibility | paths, windows, periods, and options are explicit |

::: {.notes}
A strong submission explains why each component is useful and what uncertainty remains.
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Main conclusions

1. Adjust known measurement effects before decomposition.
2. Use transformations when variation changes with the level.
3. Additive and multiplicative decompositions imply different units.
4. Moving averages reveal trend but create endpoint and smoothing trade-offs.
5. Classical decomposition assumes fixed seasonality and is not robust.
6. Seasonally adjusted data still contain the remainder.
7. STL allows controllable trend and evolving seasonality.
8. Robust STL protects components, not the observed outlier itself.
9. Component plots require careful attention to vertical scales.
10. Decomposition is a hypothesis-producing visual analysis, not causal proof.

::: {.notes}
Ask students to distinguish trend-cycle from seasonally adjusted data before ending the lecture.
:::

## Final checklist

- [ ] Is the frequency and seasonal period explicit?
- [ ] Are known calendar and scale effects adjusted?
- [ ] Is the transformation valid for the data domain?
- [ ] Is additive or multiplicative structure justified?
- [ ] Does the moving-average window match the seasonal period?
- [ ] Are endpoint losses visible?
- [ ] Can seasonality evolve over time?
- [ ] Were robust and non-robust results compared?
- [ ] Does the remainder retain structure?
- [ ] Are component scales and units communicated honestly?

::: {.notes}
This checklist can be reused for forecasting projects and decomposition-based dashboards.
:::
